seoDescription: Learn how to quickly and easily build a REST API in Java using the Spring Boot framework. This tutorial guides you through setting up a new Spring project with the Spring Web dependency and structuring your application into a controller, model, and service layer. You'll see how to create a data model for a user, implement a @RestController with a @GetMapping to handle GET requests, and inject a service using constructor injection. The example demonstrates fetching user data and testing the API endpoint with Postman.

chapters.title: Project Setup with Spring Initializr
chapters.description: Learn how to create a new Spring Boot project using the Spring Initializr and add the necessary Spring Web dependency.

chapters.title: Structuring the Application
chapters.description: This chapter covers setting up a clean project architecture with packages for the API (controller, model) and the service layer.

chapters.title: Creating the Component Classes
chapters.description: This section shows how to create the initial Java classes for the User controller, User model, and User service.

chapters.title: Defining the User Model and Annotating Components
chapters.description: See how to create the User data model POJO and annotate the controller and service classes with @RestController and @Service respectively.

chapters.title: Building the REST Controller Endpoint
chapters.description: This section demonstrates how to implement a GET endpoint in the controller using @GetMapping, accept input via @RequestParameter, and inject the service dependency.

chapters.title: Implementing the Service Layer Logic
chapters.description: Learn how to implement the business logic in the service layer, including simulating a database with a List and searching for a specific user.

chapters.title: Handling Nulls with Optional
chapters.description: Refine the code by using Java's Optional to gracefully handle cases where a requested user is not found in the data source.

chapters.title: Testing the API with Postman
chapters.description: This chapter walks through running the Spring Boot application and using Postman to test the REST API endpoint with both valid and invalid user IDs.

chapters.title: Final Review and Conclusion
chapters.description: The video concludes with a summary of the key concepts covered, including the controller-service architecture, dependency injection, and the power of Spring Boot for building APIs.

summary:
## Project Setup
To begin, create a new **Spring Boot** project using the **Spring Initializr**.

- **Project**: Maven
- **Language**: Java
- **Dependency**: Add **Spring Web** to enable web and REST API functionalities.

## Application Architecture
The project follows a standard three-tier architecture:

- **Model**: A plain Java class (`User`) that defines the data structure. It contains fields like `userID`, `name`, `age`, and `email`, along with a constructor, getters, and setters.
- **Controller**: A class annotated with `@RestController` (`UserController`) that handles incoming HTTP requests and exposes API endpoints.
- **Service**: A class annotated with `@Service` (`UserService`) that contains the core business logic, separating it from the web layer.

## Implementing the REST Endpoint
The controller is responsible for defining the API endpoints.

- **`@GetMapping("/user")`**: This annotation maps HTTP GET requests for the `/user` path to a specific method in the controller.
- **`@RequestParameter`**: This annotation is used to extract query parameters from the URL (e.g., `?id=1`) and pass them as method arguments.
- **Dependency Injection**: The `UserService` is injected into the `UserController` using **constructor injection** and the `@Autowired` annotation. This is a core principle of Spring for managing dependencies and promoting loose coupling.

> [!TIP]
> > Constructor injection is the recommended way to inject dependencies in Spring as it ensures that the required dependencies are available when the object is created.

## Service Layer and Data Handling
The service layer contains the logic for retrieving data.

- **Mock Data**: To simulate a database, a `private List<User>` is used to store user records in memory.
- **Data Retrieval Logic**: The `getUser(id)` method iterates through the list to find a user matching the provided ID.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> For a real-world application, this service would interact with a persistent data store like a SQL or NoSQL database, likely using Spring Data JPA or a similar ORM framework.

## Graceful Error Handling with `Optional`
To handle cases where a requested user might not exist, the `Optional` class is used.

- The `UserService` returns an **`Optional<User>`** instead of a `User` object directly.
- In the controller, you check if a value is present using `optional.isPresent()` before attempting to retrieve it with `optional.get()`.
- This practice helps prevent `NullPointerException`s and makes the code's intent clearer. If the user is not found, the API can return `null` or, more appropriately, a specific HTTP status code like `404 Not Found`.

## Testing the API
Once the application is running, you can test the API using a tool like **Postman**.

- **Default Port**: Spring Boot applications run on `localhost:8080` by default.
- **Sample GET Request**: `http://localhost:8080/user?id=1`
- **Testing Scenarios**:
  - Use a valid ID to confirm you receive a JSON object with the correct user data and a `200 OK` status.
  - Use an invalid ID to see how the API responds (in this case, it returns an empty body or `null`).
